segments.text: We're nearly there. But before we say goodbye, there's one last building that deserves your attention.
In front of us is the Palazzo Comunale, the town hall.
We saw it a little earlier, when we were trying to make out the Twin Towers.
Now, though, let's look at the palace itself.
At first glance, you might think it's a single building.
Of course, after the walk we've had, you know not to put too much trust in first impressions.
What you see took shape at different times, bringing together medieval buildings and alterations made between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries.
From the second half of the seventeenth century, these rooms housed the chancery.
The chancellor looked after documents and statutes, kept registers and dealt with many aspects of local administration.
Previously, meetings of the officials had been held in Palazzo Pretorio.
After sixteen sixty-one, they began taking place in the chancellor's house instead.
The administration of the territory was finding a new home.
And the building changed along with its functions.
The Twin Towers gradually became part of the complex, the rooms were enlarged and the façade was given a more regular appearance.
In seventeen eighty-two, they even decided to demolish part of the old walls and the gateway arch that stood beside the chancery.
The reason? To give the building more air.
After everything I've told you about the importance of fortifications, you'll understand that I wouldn't have taken that decision particularly lightly.
Fortunately, though, those walls no longer had to protect a besieged stronghold.
The town had other needs.
Today, this palace is the seat of the Municipality of Vicopisano.
In the rooms that once housed the chancellor, the territory is still administered, though with institutions, responsibilities and citizens very different from those I knew.
At the start of our walk, just after returning to Vicopisano, I thought I'd take the measure of the town by looking at what remained of my own work.
And my work has stood up rather well, I must admit.
But along the way, I've also encountered what was here before me.
Now it's clear to me that my Rocca is only one part of Vicopisano's history.
An important part.
A very important part.
But not the only one.
A medieval town can preserve its walls and become nothing more than a picturesque backdrop.
That hasn't happened here.
People still live and work inside these buildings.
Shops, markets, associations and local clubs keep the town alive with exhibitions, performances, gatherings and celebrations throughout the year.
Perhaps the way Vicopisano was built has helped make that possible.
The close-knit streets.
The squares.
The buildings standing close together.
But stones alone aren't enough.
A town stays alive because people keep choosing it, living in it and caring for it.
I designed Vicopisano to withstand sieges.
After nearly six hundred years, I've discovered it still holds out in another way:
by remaining a living town.
And now, sadly, we must part.
Your architecture lesson is over for today.
If you're still curious and want to discover everything Vicopisano has to offer, head to the Tourist Information Office in the municipal library, at the foot of the Clock Tower.
You can ask about visits to the Rocca, Palazzo Pretorio, the Camminamento del Soccorso and the Clock Tower.
Or choose a walk on Monte Pisano, or find out about upcoming festivals and events.
After nearly six hundred years, I'd say I've done enough walking for one day.
And then, modestly speaking, an architecture lesson like that calls for a little rest.
